dateline: MONDAY, NOVEMBER 9, 2026 · Pre-Dawn: Last Week in Review + the Weekend
headline: CHICAGO SOLD THE HANDSHAKE. THE WEEKEND SOUNDED LIKE WAR.

bullets.html: Dec Chicago closed Friday at $5.90½, down 8¾¢, after trading to $5.85, through Wednesday's $5.91 floor. Down 13¢ on the week: a tenth straight losing week by our count. KC $6.31¾ (−3½), Minneapolis $6.15¼ (−4½). Sunday night it poked to $5.94, couldn't hold, and was $5.88¼ (−2¼¢) at 12:55 a.m. Pacific. Friday's $5.85 low is intact.

Paris went the other way Friday: €225.50, up €2.75, a €7 recovery off a €218.50 morning low. From the Sept. 2 highs, Chicago is down 25.7%. Paris is down 9.7%. Those are two very different reads on the same war.

Abu Dhabi opens tomorrow. President Trump said Thursday a Russia–Ukraine deal is "very close." Then, overnight Friday into Saturday, Russia hit Kyiv with 36 ballistic missiles (ISW). Chicago sold the handshake. No ship has moved.

U.S. wheat inspections for the week ended Oct. 29: 75,413 tonnes, about 2.8 million bushels. That's the lowest week since record-keeping began in 1983 (USDA FGIS via UkrAgroConsult). This morning's number says whether it was a gap or a trend.
Russia's government offered its own farmers about $3.76 a bushel for Class 3 wheat. Most of them didn't sell.

October jobs came in at 165,000 against roughly 65,000 expected. The dollar index hit 102.28, a three-week high, and December hike odds are back above 75%. Brent slid to about $97 early Monday after its worst week since 2020.
Portland soft white bid $6.20 for November, about 29½¢ over Dec Chicago. On Oct. 23 it was even.
Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Friday was the 23rd straight close below the Suspend/Execute line, now $6.86¾, 96¼¢ overhead. Box-o-Rox informs; the marketing plan decides. See the chart and the rules →

Ahead: Today, inspections at 8 a.m. Pacific and crop progress this afternoon. Tomorrow, WASDE at 9 a.m. Pacific (the trade's average guess for U.S. wheat ending stocks is 744.1 million bu vs. USDA's 740) and the Abu Dhabi talks open the same day. Friday, COT.

body.html: Two weeks ago we wrote that the market heard half a sentence out of Moscow and sold it. Last week it got the whole paragraph, with a city, a date, two delegations and an American in the chair, and it sold that too. Dec Chicago opened the week with a 3¢ bounce Monday to $6.06½. It gave back 6¾¢ Tuesday when Washington announced the Abu Dhabi talks, then drifted Wednesday and Thursday. On Thursday, after meeting Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House, President Trump told reporters a deal was "very close" and would "involve more than Ukraine." The overnight session took him at his word. Dec traded $6.02¼ in the first half hour Thursday night and $5.85 by 8 a.m. Eastern Friday, through Wednesday's $5.91 floor, half an hour before the October jobs report came out. The report sent the dollar to a three-week high, but wheat had already done its selling: the day session bounced to $5.99½, then faded into a $5.90½ close, down 8¾¢ and still under the old floor. That puts Dec $2.04½ under the Sept. 2 high of $7.95, down 25.7%. By our count, it was the tenth straight losing week. Bloomberg called the eighth the longest losing streak since 1997. Nobody has named the tenth yet.

Then came the weekend, and Sunday night's session opened on it. Dec Chicago opened at $5.91, half a cent over Friday's close, and pushed to $5.94 inside the first 90 minutes, up through the $5.91 ceiling. It couldn't stay there. By 1 a.m. Eastern it had slipped back under, and at 12:55 a.m. Pacific it was $5.88¼, down 2¼¢, after a session low of $5.87. Friday's $5.85 low hasn't been tested. This wasn't a sleepy Sunday, either: about 7,800 contracts changed hands through 4 a.m. Eastern, against roughly 4,400 at the same point a week earlier. Somebody showed up to sell the bounce. Corn and soybeans firmed slightly overnight, per Trading Economics. Oil kept sliding: Brent traded $96.91 at 0629 GMT, down 1.5%, per Reuters.

Scout all four exchanges and you hear one story, and that's the part worth sitting with. Every market we chart closed last week below its Box-o-Rox line: Chicago by 96¼¢, Kansas City by $1.12 ($6.31¾ against $7.43¾), and Paris by €11 (€225.50 against €236.50). Every one of them has broken the long regression line that carried it up off last year's lows: Chicago's 278-session line and KC's 269-day line, both drawn from the Oct. 14, 2025 low; Minneapolis's 203-day line from its Jan. 16 low; and Paris's 232-day line. And the three U.S. contracts are all riding down short-term trendlines drawn from their late-August high closes: 50 sessions in Chicago, 49 days in KC, 45 in Minneapolis. That is timeframe harmony, exactly what the Warm Signal is built to detect. This time the harmony is in a minor key. For a seller who has been in EXECUTE since September, that's not bad news. It's confirmation that the plan has been in phase with the market instead of fighting it.

Now for the oddball. Paris didn't get the memo. Euronext milling wheat traded down to €218.50 Friday morning, then turned around and closed at €225.50, up €2.75 and €7 off its low. Our chart converts that gain at Friday's exchange rate: about a penny a bushel lower in dollars, because the dollar's three-week high ate the euro gain. Fair enough. The bigger number is the one that should stop you. From the Sept. 2 highs, Chicago is down 25.7%. Paris matched its September high again on Oct. 14–15 at €249.75 and is down only 9.7%. The dollar index is up about 4% on the whole year. Currency can't explain a 16-point gap. Paris is the market that sits closest to the Black Sea and competes head to head with Russian wheat in North Africa, and it is the one least convinced that peace is coming. Chicago, carrying an 88,726-contract fund short, is the one most convinced. One of them is reading Abu Dhabi wrong. We start finding out which tomorrow.

Here's what's actually on the table. Last Tuesday, U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff said the U.S. will mediate talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10–11, per Axios. The Kremlin confirmed that Vladimir Medinsky will lead its delegation. These are the first talks in about nine months. The announced agenda is post-war security arrangements, de-escalation and humanitarian efforts, per Fox News. Grain lanes aren't on it by name. Putin still hasn't agreed to a ceasefire, per the Kyiv Post, and Russia's deputy foreign minister, Alexander Alimov, said Oct. 26 that he sees no prospects for reviving the grain deal, per Interfax. Shipments through the Azov and Black Sea ports have been largely stopped since mid-August. Two weeks ago the market sold a "maybe." Last week it sold a meeting. Neither one has loaded a vessel.

The weekend didn't sound like a peace table. Overnight Friday into Saturday, Russia hit Kyiv with 36 ballistic missiles, per the Institute for the Study of War. Zelenskyy put the drone count at 172 on top of that, and Moscow said the target was the Trypilska thermal power plant. In Zaporizhzhia, guided bombs struck a shelter where people were waiting for aid. Ukraine's emergency service counts at least 50 dead, and on Sunday a Russian drone hit the rescue crews at the same site, per the Washington Post. Zelenskyy says Russia is stepping up the attacks to pressure Ukraine before the talks. None of it touched a grain terminal, and all of it landed after Friday's close. But it's what both delegations carry into the room tomorrow, and it's a long way from "very close."

We've seen this movie before. In the summer of 2022, wheat came down hard on the road to the original Black Sea Grain Initiative and kept selling the idea of open lanes long after the deal was signed. Then, on the last weekend of October 2022, Russia walked out of the deal. On Monday, Oct. 31, Chicago jumped close to 6% in one session. Moscow walked back in two days later, and the jump went back where it came from. The lesson isn't that deals fail. The market prices the handshake early and the walkout late, and the walkout arrives all at once. Funds held 88,726 contracts short in Chicago as of Nov. 3, per CFTC data. On the other side of that trade, commercials, the elevators, exporters and mills that handle the physical grain, swung to a net long of 5,525 contracts, a 13,064-contract shift in one week, per the same report as compiled by Ag Optimus. The hands that touch the wheat are leaning one way while the funds press the other. A stall in Abu Dhabi would meet a crowd that has to buy its way out. We aren't forecasting that. But a risk that no one is pricing is the one worth knowing about.

Read the behavior, not the headline. The most honest behavior of the past two weeks came from Russia's own farmers. Moscow opened state intervention buying on Oct. 29 at 11,100 rubles a tonne for Class 3 wheat. That's about $138 a tonne, roughly $3.76 a bushel, per UkrAgroConsult. Only a fraction of the target volume traded. Too few elevators are accredited, especially in the south, and analysts had already said it would take at least 10 MMT of state buying to steady domestic prices against a program capped at 3 MMT. Set that farm-gate offer against Russia's Baltic export quotes, which sit far above it. Freight and handling eat part of that gap in any year. Much of the rest is what a blocked port costs a Russian farmer. And the Baltic route Moscow has leaned on since August heads into ice season this winter. So most of them kept their wheat. That cuts both ways, and both ways are worth saying out loud. While the lanes stay shut, that grain is stranded. If the lanes open, it comes fast. Stored Russian wheat is the real bearish case for peace, and it's sitting in bins, not on a screen.

Meanwhile the docks here at home went quiet. Wheat inspected for export in the week ended Oct. 29 came to 75,413 tonnes, about 2.8 million bushels. That's the smallest week since record-keeping began in 1983, and 78.5% below the same week a year ago, per USDA FGIS via UkrAgroConsult. Mexico was the top destination at 38,600 tonnes. Season-to-date inspections are 7.5 MMT, 22% below the five-year average, per USDA's Grain Transportation Report. Before anybody reads the obituary, remember that inspections count what ships and sales count what's sold. Net sales for the week ended Oct. 22 were 849,800 tonnes, a marketing-year high led by the Philippines and South Korea, and that wheat hasn't shipped yet. Net sales for the week ended Oct. 29 cooled to 540,000 tonnes. One record-low week can be a gap in the loading schedule. Two would be a trend. This morning's number, at 8 a.m. Pacific, starts to tell us which. And go back to Paris for a second: if U.S. wheat has fallen 16 points further than European wheat since Labor Day, buyers have noticed. The sales should follow the price. If they don't, that's a story too.

The scissors closed, but from the wrong blade. Two weeks ago, energy was pricing a wider war while wheat priced a peace. Last week oil came down to meet wheat. Brent had its biggest weekly drop since 2020, more than 16%, on hopes for a U.S.–Iran deal, per CNBC. WTI settled at $90.83 Friday, about $11 under where it sat on Oct. 27. The weekend added to it. On Sunday Trump told CNN that new strikes on Iran are "highly unlikely" to be necessary if Tehran signs "a very strong agreement," and Brent slipped another 1.5% early Monday, even with Iran claiming, without confirmation, that tankers struck mines near Hormuz. Wheat didn't rally to meet crude; crude fell to meet wheat. Cheaper oil should eventually cool the inflation that pushed the Fed to raise rates in September, but "eventually" isn't this week. The Fed held at 3.75% to 4% on Oct. 28 by a 10–2 vote, with Governors Cook and Hammack dissenting in favor of a hike. Chair Kevin Warsh said he'd wait for an "information-rich" period before moving again. Friday delivered information: 165,000 jobs against about 65,000 expected. The dollar index rose 0.72% to 102.28 and the 10-year yield climbed to 4.87%, per Rio Times. Wheat had done its selling before the number hit, so the dollar was the second blow, not the first. But every tick on that index makes a bushel of U.S. wheat a little harder to sell overseas. The Fed meets next on Dec. 8–9. Last Tuesday's midterms, per ABC News projections, also put new leadership over both chambers of Congress in January, which means new committee chairs on the farm and trade calendar in 2027.

Our class held its bid again. Northwest Grain Growers bid November soft white at $6.20 for Portland delivery last Tuesday and again Friday. On Oct. 23 that bid sat even with Dec Chicago. On Oct. 26 it was 9½¢ over. Friday it was about 29½¢ over. The buyers behind soft white still want the wheat at this price, and the board keeps falling out from under them. Kansas City gave us a different lesson. On Oct. 27 we wrote that one strong KC session might be the first sign that the selling there was tiring. It wasn't. KC lost about 12½¢ on the week, nearly matching Chicago, and its premium over Chicago ended the week at 41¼¢, close to where it started. Funds added to their KC short. We called it one session at the time, and one session is all it turned out to be.
Scout the terrain, redrawn. These levels are for Dec Chicago.

Overhead: $5.91 comes first. It was Wednesday's floor and now it's the first ceiling. Next is $6.00 to $6.02¼, Friday's open and high, which is where the selling started; the 50-session downtrend line runs right through that zone. Beyond that, the Aug. 6–11 lows at $6.26¾.
Underfoot: Friday's $5.85, then the June 15 summer low at $5.70 on our continuation chart, then the April 10 low at $5.67½.

A close under $5.85 says the market has accepted lower prices. A close back over $6.02¼ says Friday was a probe. In Minneapolis, the line to watch is $5.98½, the Feb. 27 level, 16¾¢ below Friday's close. Friday's low of $6.12¼ stopped right at the June shelf near $6.13. In Kansas City, the June 30 low at $6.11 is 20¾¢ below. It's a map, not a forecast.

Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Friday was the 23rd straight close below the Suspend/Execute line, which now sits at $6.86¾, 96¼¢ above the market. No discretionary hold is in effect. A return to SUSPEND would take a close back above that line, and that's a long climb from here. The benchmark's record is on the chart: 83% of the 2026 crop was priced as of Oct. 1.
Marketing posture: EXECUTE, on plan. Don't let one Tuesday do the plan's job.

• Producers: The board is weak and the basis is strong. That's the exact combination a basis contract was built for: lock the Portland premium now and price the futures later. This isn't a call; it's a question to put to your plan. If you have unpriced wheat waiting on a better board, does a basis about 29½¢ over Dec argue for capturing that piece today, before tomorrow's two tables? Be clear-eyed about the trade-off: a basis contract keeps you exposed if futures keep falling. Ask your elevator whether it's writing basis contracts at these levels, and at what fee. Resting offers stay where the plan put them, and the first overhead rung is now $5.91 to $6.02¼.

• Unpriced wheat in the bin: Two weeks ago we said to run the carry against the note after the Fed. The Fed held, so the note didn't change. After Friday's jobs report, the chance that it changes in December went up. Run the carry again with a quarter point added to the operating line. If the ladder no longer clears the interest, the bin is costing you money to sit.

• Millers, feeders and end users: The coverage decision belongs before tomorrow, not after it. Two events land on the same session. The WASDE is expected to be quiet; Pro Farmer puts the spread of analyst estimates for wheat at just 7.3%. Abu Dhabi is anything but quiet, and the weekend made that plainer. Dec is $2.04½ under its Sept. 2 high with a crowded fund short underneath it. If your coverage is thin, extending it in scale before tomorrow is the protective step. If you're covered through the first quarter, there's nothing to do but watch.

• Merchandisers: Watch five things this week:
  – This morning's inspections: was 2.8 million bushels a gap or a trend?
  – Tomorrow's WASDE numbers for Russia and Argentina, not just the U.S. balance sheet.
  – The first readouts from Abu Dhabi on Wednesday morning.
  – The Paris–Chicago gap: if Europe keeps holding while Chicago slides, the export sales should show it.
  – The dollar index against its Oct. 14 high of 102.735.

• Lenders and elevator managers: Mark unpriced inventory at $5.90½, then run it at $5.85 and at $5.70. Run operating lines a quarter point higher for December. And plan for spring input requests to come in heavier than last year's. Here's why.

Retail anhydrous cost $1,007 a ton in the last week of October, up 3% in a month, and all eight fertilizers DTN tracks cost more than a year ago, per DTN. At Friday's Portland bid, that ton of anhydrous costs about 162 bushels of soft white, and that's before freight back to the farm. Oil came off $11 a barrel last week. The fertilizer bill didn't follow it down. That's the squeeze, measured in the only unit that matters at the kitchen table.

Now go back to those Russian farmers. Their own government offered them about $3.76 a bushel, and most of them said no. They aren't being stubborn. They have a number, and a reason to wait for it. The lesson for us isn't to hold. It's to have a number, and you already do. Yours were written before anybody set a table in Abu Dhabi, before tomorrow's numbers were printed, before a jobs report moved the dollar, and before a weekend of missiles reminded everyone how far "very close" can be from closed. That's exactly when they should have been written. Some of those numbers say sell, and EXECUTE says those are live. Tomorrow brings a negotiating table in Abu Dhabi and a table of numbers from Washington. Neither one knows what's on your operating note, or whose boots will be standing in that field after yours. Your plan does. Work it.

This stuff is trackable. Let's track it.
Stay tuned.
—Gabe
